title: How bursty star formation shapes spectral diversity at high redshifts: breaking degeneracies in early galaxy formation
comment: 30 pages, 16 figures. Submitted to ApJ. Comments welcome
summary: JWST has revealed an unexpected abundance of z>10 galaxies and striking spectral diversity. Here, we model bursty star formation histories (SFHs) to explore how they shape this diversity and whether spectroscopy can discriminate between explanations for the UV luminosity function (UVLF) excess. We find strong burstiness ($σ_{UV}(M_h=10^{10}M_\odot)$~0.9 mag), increasing toward low halo masses, is required to reproduce the z~6 UVLF and observed fractions of galaxies in recent star formation upturns and downturns, traced by SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}$. This burstiness naturally reproduces UVLFs and SFR upturn and downturn fractions over z~6-11. With increasing redshift, we predict galaxies in recent upturns (SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}>5$) increasingly dominate the UVLF bright end, reflecting rising accretion rates and burstier low-mass halos. This results in higher median emission-line equivalent widths (EWs), bluer UV slopes and weaker Balmer breaks at fixed $M_{UV}$, while distributions of these properties broaden. We find the downturn fraction (SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}<0.2$) is particularly sensitive to stochasticity: increasing towards faint $M_{UV}$ if burstiness increases in lower mass halos, and evolving with redshift only if stochasticity does. However, the model underpredicts the z~14 UVLF, so we explore two models which match the UVLF: increased burstiness and increased star formation efficiency. From z=10 to 14, at fixed $M_{UV}$, increased burstiness predicts the downturn fraction increases by ~2x and the weak-emitter fraction (H$β$ EW<50Å) by ~1.5x. By contrast, the increased efficiency model predicts a constant downturn fraction and declining weak-emitter fraction. Overall, our results indicate burstiness is important for explaining spectral diversity and evolution at z~6-14, and that spectroscopic samples spanning a broad $M_{UV}$ range can establish its role in the z~14 UVLF excess.

AI.tldr: Bursty star formation histories explain the spectral diversity of z>10 galaxies, and spectroscopy can distinguish whether burstiness or enhanced efficiency drives the z~14 UVLF excess.
AI.motivation: JWST revealed an unexpected abundance of z>10 galaxies and striking spectral diversity. The origin of this diversity and the nature of the UV luminosity function (UVLF) excess remain unclear, and it is unknown whether spectroscopy can discriminate between competing explanations.
AI.method: The authors model bursty star formation histories (SFHs), quantifying burstiness via the scatter in UV magnitude sigma_UV at fixed halo mass, and compare predicted UVLFs and SFR3/SFR50 upturn/downturn fractions to observations over z~6-11. They then test two models matching the z~14 UVLF—increased burstiness versus increased star formation efficiency—predicting emission-line EWs, UV slopes, Balmer breaks, and weak-emitter fractions.
AI.result: Strong burstiness (sigma_UV ~0.9 mag at M_h=10^10 M_sun), increasing toward low halo masses, is required to reproduce the z~6 UVLF and observed upturn/downturn fractions, and naturally reproduces these from z~6-11. Galaxies in recent upturns increasingly dominate the UVLF bright end with redshift, producing higher median emission-line EWs, bluer UV slopes, and weaker Balmer breaks at fixed M_UV, with broadening distributions. The downturn fraction is highly sensitive to stochasticity. The model underpredicts the z~14 UVLF; from z=10 to 14 at fixed M_UV, the increased-burstiness model predicts ~2x higher downturn fraction and ~1.5x higher weak-emitter fraction (H-beta EW<50 Å), whereas increased efficiency predicts a constant downturn fraction and declining weak-emitter fraction.
AI.conclusion: Burstiness is important for explaining spectral diversity and evolution at z~6-14. Spectroscopic samples spanning a broad M_UV range can establish its role in the z~14 UVLF excess, with downturn and weak-emitter fractions serving as discriminating diagnostics.

title: Gaia's dark partners: A new signature of dissipative dark matter
comment: 26 pages, 8 figures
summary: The Gaia mission has greatly improved our understanding of the stellar binary population. Beyond providing an extensive catalog of binary systems with two luminous stars, Gaia has also discovered several systems that appear to be star--black hole (BH) binaries. One of the leading candidate formation channels for these systems is dynamical exchange, in which one component of a star--star binary is ejected from the system and replaced by a BH. Exchange processes are very sensitive to the velocity distribution of the incoming objects, and become very efficient in the limit that perturbers are slow, so the exchanged binary population is a sensitive probe of slow-moving objects. A population of slow-moving, nonluminous objects is naturally produced in dissipative dark matter (DDM) scenarios, where a subcomponent of dark matter can cool to form a dark disk and dark compact objects (DCOs), including but not limited to BHs, with a small velocity dispersion. In this work, we evaluate the rate at which DCOs formed by DDM exchange into star--star binaries to form star--DCO binaries. We find that in a wide range of parameter space, even under conservative assumptions, the rate of exchange interactions is sufficient to produce the objects that Gaia has observed to date. In some portions of parameter space, the predicted exchange rate is well in excess of the rate estimated from observations. We point out the potential for competitive constraints on the DDM parameter space with current and future data, making the Gaia mission an important testbed for dark sector cooling.

AI.tldr: Gaia-discovered star–black hole binary candidates can be produced by dynamical exchange with dissipative-dark-matter compact objects; the predicted exchange rates match or exceed observations, enabling competitive DDM constraints.
AI.motivation: Gaia revealed candidate star–BH binaries whose formation channel is unclear; dynamical exchange favors slow perturbers, so these systems could probe a population of slow, nonluminous objects.
AI.method: Dissipative dark matter (DDM) naturally yields a cooled dark disk of dark compact objects (DCOs) with low velocity dispersion. The authors compute the rate at which DCOs exchange into star–star binaries, forming star–DCO binaries, across DDM parameter space.
AI.result: Over a wide parameter range, even under conservative assumptions, exchange rates suffice to produce the Gaia-observed systems; in parts of parameter space predicted rates exceed observational estimates.
AI.conclusion: Exchange-sensitive star–DCO binaries offer a novel probe of dark sector cooling; Gaia data provide competitive constraints on DDM parameter space.

title: Tiny Galaxies, Mighty Nitrogen: Linking Chemical Anomalies to Compact Galaxies at High Redshift using JWST/JADES
comment: Submitted to MNRAS, 21 pages, 9 figures
summary: The origin of anomalous chemical enrichment in high-redshift galaxies discovered by JWST remains a key question in galaxy evolution. Enhanced nitrogen abundances have been identified in several galaxies at early cosmic times, but the physical conditions driving this enrichment, and their connection to galaxy morphology, remain unclear. We test whether morphologically compact galaxies at 4 < z < 7 show stronger chemical anomalies than extended systems. Using JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopic data, we construct samples of compact and extended galaxies and analyse their rest-frame spectra. We stack the spectra of each population and measure key UV and optical emission lines. We detect nitrogen emission in the compact galaxy stack, including NIV], and [NII], while also detecting key carbon and oxygen lines. The detection of [OIII]λ4363 enables a direct-Te determination of the oxygen abundance. From these measurements, we infer chemical abundance ratios, including log(N/O) and log(C/O). We find that compact galaxies exhibit elevated log(N/O) (by ~ 0.7 dex) and log(C/O) (by ~ 0.5 dex) abundance ratios relative to extended systems. The abundance patterns of compact galaxy stacks are comparable to those of previously identified individual nitrogen-enhanced galaxies at high redshift and second-generation globular-cluster stars in the Milky Way. These results suggest a possible link between galaxy compactness and chemical enrichment pathways in the early Universe. Deeper JWST NIRSpec IFU observations of compact high-redshift galaxies will be crucial for determining the origin, spatial distribution, and evolutionary significance of these abundance patterns.

AI.tldr: Comparing JWST/NIRSpec composite spectra of compact vs. extended galaxies at 4<z<7, compact systems show elevated log(N/O) by ~0.7 dex and log(C/O) by ~0.5 dex, suggesting a link between galaxy compactness and anomalous chemical enrichment in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: JWST has revealed anomalous nitrogen enrichment in several high-redshift galaxies, but the physical drivers of this enrichment and its connection to galaxy morphology are unclear. The authors ask whether morphologically compact galaxies at 4<z<7 show stronger chemical anomalies than extended systems, thereby testing compactness as a tracer of the enrichment pathway.
AI.method: Rest-frame JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy is used to build samples of compact and extended galaxies at 4<z<7. Spectra of each population are stacked, and key UV and optical emission lines are measured, including NIV], [NII], and carbon/oxygen lines. The [OIII]λ4363 detection enables a direct-Te determination of oxygen abundance, from which log(N/O) and log(C/O) are inferred.
AI.result: Nitrogen emission (NIV], [NII]) is detected in the compact stack together with key carbon and oxygen lines. Relative to extended galaxies, compact galaxies show elevated log(N/O) (~0.7 dex) and log(C/O) (~0.5 dex). The compact-stack abundance patterns resemble those of individual nitrogen-enhanced high-z galaxies and second-generation globular-cluster stars in the Milky Way.
AI.conclusion: Morphological compactness is associated with stronger chemical anomalies at 4<z<7, hinting at a link between galaxy compactness and early-Universe chemical enrichment pathways. Deeper JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations are needed to establish the origin, spatial distribution, and evolutionary significance of these abundance patterns.

title: Ly$α$ in Compact Broad-Line Emitters, Including Little Red Dots, Is More Closely Linked to the Host Galaxy than to the Broad-Line Nucleus
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to AAS journals
summary: JWST has found many faint broad-line AGN at $z>4$, but it is unclear whether the Ly$α$ we see from them comes from the accreting black hole or from its host galaxy. The answer matters for how these sources are interpreted and for how many ionizing photons they release. We use deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the DIVER program to measure Ly$α$ in 12 compact broad-line emitters (CBEs) at $z=4.2$--5.5 in GOODS-N. CBEs include little red dots (LRDs), little blue dots, and other broad-line AGN. Six are detected in Ly$α$. Every source shows a broad-line region, yet Ly$α$ does not follow it: the sources with the strongest H$α$ relative to the UV include weak detections and nondetections, and every detected Ly$α$ line (FWHM $\approx300$--1000~km~s$^{-1}$) is narrower than broad H$α$ (1100--3300~km~s$^{-1}$). Instead, Ly$α$ appears to track the host galaxy. We model the AGN-subtracted host with a dust-attenuated SED fit. Including the upper limits, the observed Ly$α$ follows the Ly$α$ production in this host model more closely than it follows H$α$/UV, in both equivalent width and luminosity. Every detection exceeds its host-model value by a factor of 1.5--18, leaving room for a nuclear contribution. The black hole is visible in these sources, but the Ly$α$ we observe is more closely tied to its host. The median effective Ly$α$ escape fraction of the detections is only 0.09, which suggests that ionizing escape from CBEs is typically modest and varies widely.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of 12 compact broad-line emitters (LRDs, little blue dots, and other broad-line AGN) at z=4.2–5.5 shows that observed Lyα tracks host-galaxy Lyα production rather than the broad-line region, implying modest and highly variable ionizing escape (median effective Lyα escape fraction ≈0.09).
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered many faint broad-line AGN at z>4, but it is unclear whether their Lyα emission originates from the accreting black hole (broad-line region) or from the host galaxy. Resolving this is essential for correctly interpreting these sources and for quantifying their ionizing photon output and escape.
AI.method: Deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the DIVER program is used to measure Lyα in 12 compact broad-line emitters (CBEs; including little red dots, little blue dots, and other broad-line AGN) at z=4.2–5.5 in GOODS-N. The AGN-subtracted host is modeled with a dust-attenuated SED fit, and observed Lyα (including upper limits) is compared against host-model Lyα production and against Hα/UV-based AGN diagnostics, in both equivalent width and luminosity.
AI.result: Six of 12 sources are detected in Lyα. All sources show a broad-line region, but Lyα does not follow it: sources with the strongest Hα relative to UV have weak or absent Lyα, and every detected Lyα line (FWHM ≈300–1000 km/s) is narrower than broad Hα (FWHM 1100–3300 km/s). Observed Lyα instead tracks the host-galaxy model more closely than it tracks Hα/UV in both EW and luminosity. Every detection exceeds its host-model value by a factor of 1.5–18, leaving room for a nuclear contribution. The median effective Lyα escape fraction among detections is only 0.09.
AI.conclusion: Although the black hole is visible in these sources, the observed Lyα is more closely tied to the host galaxy than to the broad-line region. The low median effective Lyα escape fraction (≈0.09) suggests that ionizing-photon escape from CBEs is typically modest and varies widely across the population.

title: Surface Nitrogen enrichment from the LMC to the Early Universe: the roles of rotation, overshooting and mass loss
comment: Accepted in A&A Letters, 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 appendix
summary: The strong nitrogen (N) features observed in high-redshift galaxies, such as GN-z11, with JWST point to an efficient source of N production in the early Universe. Very massive stars (VMSs) are promising candidates owing to their strong winds and large convective cores of CNO-processed material. Whether massive-star surfaces in general become N-enriched depends on the interplay of convective-boundary mixing (overshooting), rotation, and mass loss, which remains poorly constrained. Using a grid of MESA evolutionary models, we isolate the overshooting and rotation channels at $40$, $100$, and $200\,M_\odot$ and investigate how these channels bring N-rich material to the surface of massive and very massive stars as a function of initial mass and metallicity. We also construct a synthetic Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) population based on a larger initial mass grid ranging from $20-300\,M_\odot$ for comparison with the observed N-enriched fraction. VMS surface enrichment is remarkably robust across cosmic metallicity. At lower metallicities, wind stripping is weaker and the overshooting channel shuts off entirely, yet a modest amount of rotation of $\sim90\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ alone still enriches the surface. At higher metallicity, stronger winds dominate and uncover the core almost independently of the adopted mixing. The two channels operate through physically distinct mechanisms: overshooting enriches the surface only once winds strip the envelope down into the N-rich layers left by the receding core, giving an abrupt jump. Rotation, by contrast, mixes N outward continuously through the layers above the core, producing a gradual rise. Applied to the LMC, a population with modest rotation drawn from the observed velocity distribution and modest overshooting reproduces the observed N-enriched fraction without large core boundary mixing efficiencies otherwise required by non-rotating models.

AI.tldr: MESA models of 40–200 M☉ stars show that very massive stars become N-enriched robustly across metallicity via two distinct channels—convective overshooting (abrupt, wind-dependent) and rotation (gradual, wind-independent)—and a modest-rotation LMC population reproduces the observed N-enriched fraction without large boundary mixing.
AI.motivation: JWST observations of strong nitrogen features in high-redshift galaxies like GN-z11 imply an efficient early-Universe N source, and very massive stars (VMSs) with strong winds and large CNO-processed convective cores are prime candidates. However, whether massive-star surfaces become N-enriched depends on the poorly constrained interplay of convective-boundary mixing (overshooting), rotation, and mass loss.
AI.method: A grid of MESA evolutionary models at 40, 100, and 200 M☉ is used to isolate the overshooting and rotation channels and study how they transport N-rich material to the surface as a function of initial mass and metallicity. A synthetic LMC population from a 20–300 M☉ grid is also constructed and compared with the observed N-enriched fraction.
AI.result: VMS surface enrichment is robust across cosmic metallicity. At low metallicity, wind stripping is weak and the overshooting channel shuts off entirely, yet modest rotation (~90 km/s) alone still enriches the surface. At high metallicity, strong winds dominate and uncover the core almost independently of mixing. The channels are physically distinct: overshooting produces an abrupt jump once winds strip the envelope into N-rich layers, while rotation mixes N outward continuously, giving a gradual rise. The synthetic LMC population with modest rotation and modest overshooting reproduces the observed N-enriched fraction without the large core-boundary mixing efficiencies required by non-rotating models.
AI.conclusion: VMS surface N-enrichment arises robustly from two distinct, physically separable channels whose relative importance is set by metallicity, mass loss, and rotation. Modest rotation plus modest overshooting suffices to match observed LMC enrichment, reducing the need for extreme boundary-mixing efficiencies and supporting VMSs as an efficient early-Universe N source.

title: A full chemical network treatment of supermassive black hole seed formation from dark matter annihilation or decay
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures
summary: The recent discoveries of high-redshift quasars at $z\sim6-10.1$ present a challenge to conventional supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenarios: their central SMBHs are too large to have grown from early stellar remnants, even under efficient super-Eddington accretion. An alternative approach is the direct collapse of primordial, dust- and metal-free gas clouds into black hole seeds as early as $z\sim20$. To prevent fragmentation from highly efficient molecular hydrogen cooling and allow such a collapse, a strong flux of UV photons is required to photodissociate molecular hydrogen, suppressing star formation. We investigate whether the decay or annihilation of dark matter with masses below $\sim200$ eV can produce sufficient UV radiation, both from the cosmological background and within early dark matter halos. Using thermal simulations of a one-zone primordial gas cloud model with the Grackle chemistry and cooling library, we map the resulting gas behavior across a range of dark matter lifetimes, cross sections, and masses. From this, we determine regions of parameter space where direct collapse into an SMBH is possible and the corresponding maximum halo mass required.

AI.tldr: Sub-200 eV dark matter decay or annihilation may supply the UV flux needed to photodissociate H2 and enable direct collapse of primordial gas clouds into supermassive black hole seeds at high redshift.
AI.motivation: Observations of quasars at z~6-10.1 harbor SMBHs too massive to have grown from early stellar remnants, even with efficient super-Eddington accretion. Direct collapse of dust- and metal-free primordial gas into BH seeds at z~20 is an alternative, but it requires strong UV radiation to photodissociate H2 and suppress fragmentation via molecular cooling. The authors ask whether decaying or annihilating light dark matter (m < ~200 eV) can provide this UV flux.
AI.method: Thermal simulations of a one-zone primordial gas cloud model using the Grackle chemistry and cooling library, scanning over dark matter lifetime, annihilation cross section, and mass. UV production is considered both from the cosmological background and from within early DM halos; results are mapped to parameter-space regions permitting direct collapse and the corresponding maximum required halo mass.
AI.result: The paper maps dark matter (lifetime, cross section, mass) parameter space to gas behavior, identifying regions where direct collapse into an SMBH is feasible and the maximum halo mass required in each case.
AI.conclusion: Light dark matter decay/annihilation is a viable UV source for enabling direct-collapse SMBH seed formation, with the feasible parameter space and associated halo mass constraints delineated.

title: Towards Self-consistent Modeling of Quasi-Stars and their NLTE Spectra: Implications for Little Red Dots
comment: 18 pages, 12 figures
summary: Quasi-stars, massive envelopes surrounding rapidly accreting black hole (BH) seeds, are promising candidates for explaining the rapid formation of supermassive black holes in the early Universe and may account for some of the JWST-discovered Little Red Dots (LRDs). We present a self-consistent framework combining stellar evolution calculations with non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) spectral synthesis to test this connection. Our models drop the polytropic assumptions of previous work: the envelope is described entirely by mixing-length theory, with saturated convection and radiative energy setting the luminosity at an inner boundary a few hundred Schwarzschild radii from the BH. This removes the BH-mass limits of earlier models, and we follow the evolution up to BH-to-total mass ratios approaching unity. We then use TLUSTY to compute the first converged NLTE atmospheric models for the surface conditions and primordial hydrogen-helium composition expected in quasi-stars. Our models produce cool photospheres, prominent Balmer breaks, and Balmer and Paschen absorption features. NLTE effects substantially modify line strengths, increasing Balmer absorption depths by $\sim 35-55\%$ relative to LTE models, while having a minor effect on the continuum. Comparison with observed LRD spectral energy distributions shows broad agreement in continuum shape, although our models do not reproduce their commonly observed strong emission lines. Under the quasi-star interpretation, comparisons with individual LRDs suggest characteristic quasi-star masses of approximately $10^5-10^7 M_\odot$. These results establish a physically motivated connection between quasi-star evolution and observable spectra, providing a framework for testing quasi-stars as progenitors of LRDs while identifying limitations of current atmospheric models.

AI.tldr: Self-consistent quasi-star models (mixing-length envelope + TLUSTY NLTE spectra) drop polytropic assumptions, reach BH mass ratios near unity, and reproduce LRD continuum/Balmer breaks but not strong emission lines, implying quasi-star masses of ~10^5-10^7 M_sun.
AI.motivation: Quasi-stars, massive envelopes around rapidly accreting BH seeds, are candidate explanations for early-Universe supermassive BH formation and possibly JWST Little Red Dots (LRDs); the quasi-star-LRD connection needs a physically motivated, self-consistent spectral test free of prior polytropic approximations.
AI.method: Stellar evolution calculations with the envelope fully described by mixing-length theory (saturated convection, radiative energy setting luminosity at an inner boundary a few hundred Schwarzschild radii) instead of polytropes; evolution followed to BH-to-total mass ratios approaching unity. First converged NLTE atmospheric models via TLUSTY for quasi-star surface conditions and primordial H-He composition, compared with LRD SEDs.
AI.result: Models yield cool photospheres, prominent Balmer breaks, and Balmer/Paschen absorption. NLTE increases Balmer absorption depths by ~35-55% versus LTE with minor continuum effects. Continuum shape broadly agrees with LRD SEDs, but strong observed emission lines are not reproduced; implied quasi-star masses ~10^5-10^7 M_sun.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a physically motivated link between quasi-star evolution and observable spectra, providing a framework for testing quasi-stars as LRD progenitors while highlighting limitations of current atmospheric models.

title: Isophotal signatures of the brightest cluster galaxy - intracluster light transition
comment: 21 pages, 9 (main) + 7 (appendix) figures. Accepted 2026 October 8. Received 2026 September 21; in original form 2026 July 22
summary: The distinction between brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) and intracluster light (ICL) remains ambiguous, with inferred cluster properties depending strongly on the adopted definition and measurement methodology. We report the presence of a common inflection feature in the radial profiles of surface brightness, ellipticity, and position angle of BCG+ICL systems, indicative of a structural transition in the underlying stellar distribution. Using a combination of low redshift clusters (z < 0.1) observed with the Wendelstein Wide Field Imager, deep Hyper Suprime-Cam observations of clusters at 0.2 < z < 0.4, and cosmological hydrodynamical simulations from Horizon-AGN and Hydrangea, we consistently identify a common inflection at radii of 60-85 kpc. We interpret this feature as a characteristic transition in the combined BCG+ICL light distribution, that may reflect the hierarchical assembly of the cluster. The persistence of this feature across multiple photometric bands, redshift ranges, and simulations supports its robustness. To identify these transitions, we employ an automated second derivative based approach that does not rely on parametric decompositions or arbitrary surface brightness thresholds. This framework provides a physically motivated and scalable means to characterise the BCG-ICL transition, and it will be of paramount importance for forthcoming large scale surveys such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the European Space Agency's Euclid mission.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a common inflection feature at 60–85 kpc in the radial profiles of surface brightness, ellipticity, and position angle of BCG+ICL systems, identified with an automated second-derivative method across observations and simulations.
AI.motivation: The BCG/ICL distinction is ambiguous, and inferred cluster properties depend strongly on the adopted definition and measurement methodology, motivating a physically grounded, non-arbitrary characterization of the BCG–ICL transition.
AI.method: Combines low-redshift clusters (z < 0.1) from the Wendelstein Wide Field Imager, deep Hyper Suprime-Cam observations at 0.2 < z < 0.4, and cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (Horizon-AGN, Hydrangea). Transitions are detected via an automated second-derivative approach requiring no parametric decomposition or arbitrary surface-brightness thresholds.
AI.result: A consistent inflection at radii of 60–85 kpc is found in surface brightness, ellipticity, and position-angle profiles, persisting across multiple photometric bands, redshift ranges, and simulations, indicating a structural transition in the stellar distribution.
AI.conclusion: The inflection is interpreted as a characteristic transition in the combined BCG+ICL light distribution, possibly reflecting hierarchical cluster assembly. The framework offers a physically motivated, scalable means to characterize the BCG–ICL transition, relevant for LSST and Euclid.

title: Shadowing the Sun I: Testing Synthetic Granulation Spectra with NEID Solar Eclipse Observations
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: The subtle Doppler radial velocity (RV) signature of an Earth-mass exoplanet in the Habitable Zone around a nearby Sun-like star is difficult to detect due to stellar variability. While multiple techniques aim to mitigate rotationally-modulated stellar activity, granulation, introducing 0.1-1 m s$^{-1}$ RV shifts, currently sets the floor for detecting Earth-mass RV signals for low-activity stars. Observations of the Rossiter-McLaughlin (RM) effect during a solar eclipse, with a peak-to-trough amplitude of $\sim$1.4 km s$^{-1}$, are a rigorous test of granulation and convective blueshift in the solar spectrum. Using NEID solar feed data of the October 2023 solar eclipse and GRASS-E (a geometry-modified version of GRASS), we compare the observed RVs for 22 lines with the simulated RVs from the synthetic granulation-driven spectra. Residuals of the GRASS-E Fe I 5434 angstrom model show an RMS of 13.47 m s$^{-1}$ over the RM signal. We find that a model with an optimized convective blueshift polynomial for Fe I 5434 significantly outperforms GRASS-E with an RMS of only 2.90 m s$^{-1}$, suggesting that GRASS-E is currently limited by sparse center-to-limb observations. By combining a set of spectral lines, we achieve a weighted RMS of 5.2 m s$^{-1}$ over the RM signal ($\sim$0.37\%), a level of accuracy well beyond the reach of current exoplanet transit observations. In all, we demonstrate that solar eclipse observations allow us to recover the center-to-limb variation of the convective blueshift for individual spectral lines.

AI.tldr: Using NEID solar feed observations of the October 2023 solar eclipse, the authors test granulation-driven RV models via the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect, showing that optimized convective blueshift models recover solar center-to-limb variation to a weighted RMS of ~5.2 m/s.
AI.motivation: Granulation introduces 0.1–1 m/s RV shifts that currently set the detection floor for Earth-mass exoplanets in the Habitable Zone of low-activity Sun-like stars, and understanding convective blueshift and granulation is essential to push below this limit.
AI.method: The RM effect during the October 2023 solar eclipse (peak-to-trough ~1.4 km/s) provides a stringent test. Using NEID solar feed data and GRASS-E (a geometry-modified GRASS), the authors compare observed RVs for 22 spectral lines against simulated granulation-driven spectra, and fit an optimized convective blueshift polynomial for Fe I 5434 Å.
AI.result: GRASS-E Fe I 5434 Å residuals show 13.47 m/s RMS over the RM signal; the optimized convective blueshift polynomial reduces this to 2.90 m/s, indicating GRASS-E is limited by sparse center-to-limb observations. Combining multiple lines yields a weighted RMS of 5.2 m/s (~0.37% of the RM signal).
AI.conclusion: Solar eclipse observations enable recovery of the center-to-limb variation of convective blueshift for individual spectral lines, achieving accuracy beyond current exoplanet transit observations and advancing granulation modeling for precise RV work.

title: Galactic-Scale Distribution of 10Be and Its Implications for the Early Solar System 10Be/9Be
comment: 28 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Meteoritic inclusions indicate that the early Solar System contained a substantial abundance of the short-lived radionuclide 10Be. Whether it was inherited from the parent molecular cloud or requires local irradiation or late injection remains debated. Here we present the first three-dimensional simulations of a Milky Way-like disc that follow the multi-phase interstellar medium, cosmic rays (CRs), and the production and transport of 10Be by galactic CRs (GCRs) and in supernova remnants (SNRs). Nearly all 10Be is produced by GCR interactions; SNRs contribute at most about ten percent of the 10Be inherited by newly formed stars. The 10Be/9Be ratio traces the CR energy density, declining smoothly with galactocentric radius, and because stars form where supernovae inject CRs, their natal gas is CR-enriched roughly fivefold relative to the mean interstellar medium, which one-zone estimates miss. Accounting for a possibly higher Galactic star formation rate 4.6 Gyr ago, inheritance of GCR-produced 10Be can then explain the early Solar System's 10Be/9Be in our models, without late injection or local irradiation. Even when GCR-induced 10Be production in dense gas is reduced tenfold, the meteoritic value is reached in the innermost disc and missed by only a factor of a few elsewhere, so the main conclusion is robust to uncertain low-energy GCR penetration. The inferred birth radius of the Sun depends strongly on the CR diffusivity, ranging between 3 and 8 kpc, suggesting that improved modelling of low-energy CR transport could sharpen constraints on the birthplace of the Solar System.

AI.tldr: First 3D Milky Way-like disc simulations tracking multi-phase ISM, cosmic rays, and 10Be production/transport show that galactic cosmic rays, not supernovae, supply nearly all inherited 10Be, and that star-forming gas is CR-enriched ~5x, allowing inheritance of GCR-produced 10Be to explain the early Solar System's 10Be/9Be without late injection or local irradiation.
AI.motivation: Meteoritic inclusions reveal a substantial early Solar System abundance of the short-lived radionuclide 10Be, but its origin—inheritance from the parent molecular cloud versus local irradiation or late injection—remains debated. Existing one-zone estimates cannot capture the spatially resolved, multi-phase production and transport of 10Be in a galactic disc.
AI.method: Three-dimensional simulations of a Milky Way-like disc that simultaneously follow the multi-phase interstellar medium, cosmic-ray (CR) propagation, and the production and transport of 10Be by galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) and in supernova remnants (SNRs). The authors test robustness by degrading GCR-induced 10Be production in dense gas tenfold and by varying CR diffusivity.
AI.result: Nearly all 10Be is produced by GCR interactions, with SNRs contributing at most ~10% of the 10Be inherited by newly formed stars. The 10Be/9Be ratio traces CR energy density and declines smoothly with galactocentric radius; because stars form where supernovae inject CRs, natal gas is CR-enriched ~5x relative to the mean ISM—an effect one-zone estimates miss. Accounting for a possibly higher Galactic star formation rate 4.6 Gyr ago, GCR-produced 10Be inheritance reproduces the early Solar System 10Be/9Be. Even with a tenfold reduction of GCR-induced 10Be production in dense gas, the meteoritic value is reached in the innermost disc and missed by only a factor of a few elsewhere. The inferred solar birth radius ranges from 3 to 8 kpc depending strongly on CR diffusivity.
AI.conclusion: Inheritance of GCR-produced 10Be can explain the early Solar System's 10Be/9Be without invoking late injection or local irradiation, and the conclusion is robust to uncertain low-energy GCR penetration. title: Protostellar evolution of intermediate-mass stars: implications for the survival of fossil magnetic fields
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The detection of strong magnetic fields in radiative stars, particularly chemically peculiar Ap/Bp stars, has motivated various scenarios regarding their origin, including the fossil field hypothesis. We determine the characteristic mass at which intermediate-mass protostars transition from convective to radiative interiors, exploring how this transition favors magnetic field survival. Using the 1D stellar evolution code MESA, we model the pre-main-sequence evolution of intermediate-mass protostars from convective initial seeds across different metallicities, average accretion rates, and accretion histories. Accretion history details play a secondary role compared to the average rate and metallicity. Lower metallicities shift the transition to lower masses. For $Z \ge 0.01$ and accretion rates above $4 \times 10^{-6}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, models retain convective envelopes up to the end of accretion, potentially dissipating accreted magnetic flux. Because this transition typically occurs above $\sim 1.3\,M_\odot$, our results help explain the preferential survival of fossil fields in intermediate-mass stars, provided the radiative structure persists post-accretion. title: The STARfall pathway: forging intermediate-mass black holes through stellar collisions in dense star clusters
comment: 22 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables
summary: Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs, $10^2 < m_{\rm BH}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot} < 10^5$) are elusive objects bridging the gap between stellar-mass and supermassive black holes, whose origin remains uncertain. They may form from the collapse of very massive stars (VMSs, $m_*\geq150\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$) assembled through repeated stellar collisions in compact and fast evolving star clusters. We investigate the formation of VMSs and IMBH seeds via repeated mergers and collisions as a function of cluster initial conditions, assessing the implications for globular clusters and dense high-redshift system. We develop STARfall, a semi-analytic tool that follows the evolution of a massive stellar binary via binary-single interactions, mergers, collisions, and stellar evolution, while consistently accounting for the host cluster evolution. Our results show that clusters with central densities above $10^6\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{pc}^{-3}$ can undergo a catastrophic sequence of stellar collisions, or "starastrophe", within $3$ Myr. Through this process, VMSs rapidly grow in mass and collapse into IMBHs with masses of up to $10^3-10^4\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$, despite the effects of intense stellar winds. Applying our models to observed systems, we find that compact clusters in the Cosmic Gems Arc and Milky Way globular clusters could have hosted VMSs that collapsed into IMBHs in this mass range. Despite their longer core-collapse timescales, the inferred central densities of Little Red Dots may also support IMBH formation in the same mass interval. Our models show that VMS assembly requires two essential ingredients: short core-collapse times and large central densities. Compared to observed systems, our models suggest that clusters in the Cosmic Gems Arcs and several Galactic globular clusters could have nurtured VMSs that directly collapsed to IMBHs with masses $10^3-10^4\,\text{M}_{\odot}$.

AI.tldr: Compact, dense star clusters can rapidly assemble very massive stars through stellar collisions and mergers, which collapse into intermediate-mass black hole seeds of 10^3-10^4 solar masses.
AI.motivation: Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are elusive and their origin is unclear. title: A Wolf-Rayet nebula in its disruption phase: high-resolution radio observations of PCG 11
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: (abridged abstract) Wolf-Rayet stars have high mass-loss rates and fast stellar winds. Their interaction with circumstellar material from previous evolutionary phases can produce complex nebular morphologies. Hydrodynamic instabilities can fragment wind-swept material, producing condensations, filaments, and gaps that alter the confinement of stellar wind and ionizing radiation. The role of fragmentation in the late evolution and dispersal of WR nebulae remains poorly constrained. PCG 11, with its fragmented morphology and regular scalloped rim, offers an opportunity to investigate these processes. We aim to characterize the structure of PCG 11 and investigate its ring-like morphology and scalloped rim. We constrain its three-dimensional geometry and determine whether the optical fragmentation pattern is also traced by ionized gas. We obtained high-resolution radio continuum images with MeerKAT at 2.6 and 3.1 GHz and ATCA at 5.5 and 9.0 GHz. The radio emission reveals a hollow, equatorially enhanced structure viewed close to its symmetry axis. The images resolve the rim into condensations, low-brightness gaps, and finger-like protrusions. We quantify the fragmentation scale and relate it to the nebular geometry. We also detect an unresolved source coincident with WR 75ab, whose rising radio spectrum is consistent with thermal wind emission. The nebula processes only a small fraction of the stellar ionizing radiation, indicating substantial photon leakage. PCG 11 captures a poorly observed stage in massive-star bubble evolution: the swept-up shell has developed a coherent instability pattern and become fragmented and porous, while remaining dynamically coupled to the stellar wind. It provides a clear view of how fragmentation and erosion reshape the circumstellar environment during a transitional evolutionary phase.

title: Revisiting the Missing Baryon Problem: Baryon Redistribution Across Halo Evolution
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The baryon fraction provides a fundamental diagnostic of baryonic matter distribution within dark matter halos and the baryon cycle. While its cosmic value is well constrained, the baryon content within halos on nearly all scales is significantly lower than the cosmic mean; this is called the ``missing baryon problem.'' Using the high spatial, mass, and temporal resolutions of the NewCluster simulation, we investigate the baryon fraction evolution by tracing halo assembly histories from merger trees and gas tracer particles. We identify three distinct evolutionary phases: an early growth phase driven by cold accretion in low-mass halos, a suppression phase likely dominated by supernova feedback, and a recovery phase in massive halos enabled by deeper potential wells and hot-mode accretion. We further find that the redshift dependence of baryon fraction, particularly in low-mass halos, is influenced by the thermal state of the intergalactic medium, with suppression emerging after the surrounding gas becomes persistently hotter than the halo virial temperature. In addition, the scatter in baryon fraction at fixed halo mass correlates with the large-scale environment, with baryon-rich halos preferentially residing closer to filamentary structures. Overall, our results highlight that baryon fraction evolution is governed by the interplay between feedback and environment, requiring a time-resolved perspective on the baryon cycle.

AI.tldr: Using the NewCluster simulation and halo merger trees, the authors show that halo baryon fraction evolves through three phases—cold-accretion growth, supernova-feedback suppression, and massive-halo recovery—with redshift dependence driven by intergalactic medium thermal state and scatter linked to large-scale environment.
AI.motivation: The baryon content of halos on nearly all scales falls well below the cosmic mean (the "missing baryon problem"), so a time-resolved understanding of how baryon fraction evolves is needed to connect feedback, accretion, and environment.
AI.method: Trace halo assembly histories in the high-resolution NewCluster simulation using merger trees and gas tracer particles across high spatial, mass, and temporal resolution.
AI.result: Identifies three evolutionary phases: cold-accretion-driven early growth in low-mass halos, a suppression phase dominated by supernova feedback, and a recovery phase in massive halos from deeper potential wells and hot-mode accretion. Redshift dependence, especially for low-mass halos, tracks the thermal state of the intergalactic medium, with suppression appearing once surrounding gas stays hotter than the virial temperature. Baryon fraction scatter at fixed mass correlates with large-scale environment, with baryon-rich halos lying nearer filaments.
AI.conclusion: Halo baryon fraction evolution is governed by the interplay of feedback and environment, requiring a time-resolved perspective on the baryon cycle.

title: Carbon-Reaction Constraints on Stellar Evolution: White-Dwarf Heating, Carbon-Burning Products, and Black-Hole Masses
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures
summary: The effects of ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}+{}^{12}\mathrm{C}$ fusion and ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}(α,γ){}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ capture on stellar heating, composition, and black-hole masses are examined. Rates from a published Bayesian analysis of carbon fusion are used in calculations with MESA. In an accreting carbon--oxygen white dwarf, the Bayesian rates move the point at which nuclear heating equals combined neutrino and surface photon losses to slightly larger stellar masses and higher central temperatures and densities. At an accretion rate of $10^{-7}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, the Bayesian median gives a central temperature approximately $2.57\%$ higher and a central density $18.9\%$ higher than the calculation using the standard CF88 rate. A separate calculation follows carbon burning in an initially $20\,M_\odot$, $Z=0.0142$ star. Relative to the CF88 rate with MESA's standard division between proton and alpha channels, the Bayesian-median rate with the proton-to-alpha ratio of Yang et al. increases the neon-20 mass remaining at central carbon depletion by $10.8\%$ and decreases the sodium-23 mass by $28.7\%$. For helium capture on carbon, the nuclear constraint $S_{\rm tot}(300\,\mathrm{keV})=118\pm17\,\mathrm{keV\,b}$ is applied to the published $Z=10^{-5}$ stellar models of Farag et al. Linear interpolation gives a maximum black-hole mass below the pair-instability gap of approximately $61.5$--$77.4\,M_\odot$ within the assumptions of those models. New MESA calculations at $Z=0.00142$ give smaller bound masses before collapse. Differences in the stellar assumptions prevent attributing the difference between the two curves to metallicity alone.

AI.tldr: Using Bayesian ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}+{}^{12}\mathrm{C}$ rates in MESA, an accreting C-O white dwarf reaches the nuclear-heating balance point at higher central temperature (+2.57%) and density (+18.9%); in a $20\,M_\odot$ star the Bayesian median rate raises remaining ${}^{20}\mathrm{Ne}$ by 10.8% and lowers ${}^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ by 28.7%, while the constrained ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma){}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ rate yields pre-pair-instability BH masses of ~61.5–77.4 $M_\odot$.
AI.motivation: To quantify how updated nuclear reaction rates—Bayesian ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}+{}^{12}\mathrm{C}$ fusion and a constraint on ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma){}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ capture—propagate into stellar heating, nucleosynthesis, and black-hole mass outcomes, replacing reliance on the standard CF88 rates.
AI.method: MESA calculations adopting a published Bayesian analysis of carbon fusion rates; a C-O white dwarf accreting at $10^{-7}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ to locate where nuclear heating balances neutrino plus surface photon losses; a $20\,M_\odot$, $Z=0.0142$ star followed through central carbon depletion using the Yang et al. proton-to-alpha ratio; and linear interpolation of the constraint $S_{\rm tot}(300\,\mathrm{keV})=118\pm17\,\mathrm{keV\,b}$ applied to the Farag et al. $Z=10^{-5}$ models, plus new MESA runs at $Z=0.00142$.

Constraints on ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma){}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ place the maximum BH mass below the pair-instability gap within the adopted model assumptions.

title: H 0557$-$385: A Candidate Missing Link Between Radio-Quiet Seyferts and Young Radio Galaxies
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The Seyfert 1 galaxy H 0557$-$385 (z = 0.034) has long been classified as radio-quiet on the basis of its radio-to-optical flux ratio, yet its radio properties are physically inconsistent with this designation. We present a broadband ($0.076 - 258.8$ GHz) radio spectral analysis combining new Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) observations with archival Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) data. The spectrum requires a two-component model: a compact, self-absorbed component with a stratified gigahertz-peaked (GPS)/high-frequency-peaked (HFP) spectral shape (turnover at $9.4^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$ GHz), superposed on an extended, optically thin power-law lobe ($α_{\rm pl} = -0.78$) that dominates below ~1.6 GHz. The derived parameters $-$ a source size of ~15 pc, an equipartition magnetic field of 2.8 mG, a synchrotron age of $\lesssim1.8\times10^{3}$ yr, and a time-averaged jet power of ${\sim}5\times10^{41}$ $-$ $5\times10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ $-$ are characteristic of compact steep-spectrum and GPS young radio galaxies, not of canonical radio-quiet AGN. The two-component structure admits two interpretations that the present data cannot distinguish: the extended emission may be the growing lobe of a genuinely young, expanding radio galaxy, or relic plasma from an earlier episode of a transient or recurrent jet. Under either, H 0557$-$385 is better understood as an intermediate object: optically a Seyfert, but with the radio-physical properties of a newly ignited or recently re-triggered radio galaxy. It is therefore a candidate missing link between radio-quiet AGN and large-scale radio galaxies. Distinguishing these scenarios will require high-resolution imaging and multi-epoch monitoring

AI.tldr: Broadband radio spectroscopy shows that the "radio-quiet" Seyfert 1 galaxy H 0557-385 hosts a compact, self-absorbed GPS/HFP core plus an optically thin lobe with young radio galaxy energetics, making it a candidate missing link between radio-quiet AGN and radio galaxies.
AI.motivation: H 0557-385 (z = 0.034) is classified as radio-quiet by its radio-to-optical flux ratio, but its radio properties are physically inconsistent with that designation, so the classification scheme itself is suspect at the low-luminosity end.
AI.method: New ATCA observations combined with archival MWA, ASKAP and ALMA data yield a 0.076-258.8 GHz spectrum, fitted with a two-component model (self-absorbed peaked core plus optically thin lobe); physical parameters (size, equipartition field, synchrotron age, jet power) are derived.
AI.result: A stratified GPS/HFP component with turnover at 9.4(+0.6/-0.5) GHz is superposed on an optically thin power-law lobe (alpha_pl = -0.78) dominating below ~1.6 GHz. Derived values: size ~15 pc, B_eq = 2.8 mG, synchrotron age <~1.8e3 yr, time-averaged jet power ~5e41-5e44 erg/s - typical of CSS/GPS young radio galaxies.
AI.conclusion: The data cannot distinguish a genuinely young expanding radio galaxy from relic plasma of a transient/recurrent jet. Either way, H 0557-385 is optically a Seyfert but radio-physically a newly ignited or re-triggered radio galaxy, a candidate missing link; high-resolution imaging and multi-epoch monitoring are needed.

title: Up in smoke: carbon-destruction in the terrestrial planet-forming region of a young Class I disk
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Earth's surface and deep mantle are strongly depleted in carbon compared to the Sun. Sublimation of solid carbonaceous material in the inner midplanes of young disks could cause this depletion. We study such thermal processing in HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with a rich hydrocarbon spectrum. A companion paper has shown that it is recondensing refractory dust from a hot inner disk region, and that oxygen-bearing species are tracing a warm (300-500 K) molecular layer entrained in a disk-wind. In this work, we analyze the carbon species in the JWST spectrum of this source using local thermal equilibrium slab models. We detect warm (~400 K) HCN and C2H2 at the base of a disk wind, as well as colder (~40 K) C4H2, CH3, and CS in the outer disk or outflow cavity wall. Additionally, 13CCH2, CH4, and C6H2 are detected, while ALMA observations reveal C2H tracing the outflow cavity walls. We suggest that in a "refractory carbon destruction zone" in the inner disk, carbon-bearing species are released from the grains, possibly contributing to the observed carbon depletion of Earth. The disk wind then redistributes carbon carried by HCN and C2H2 from the inner disk to the colder outer disk, where UV-induced gas-phase reactions with C2H in the outflow cavity walls could produce the aliphatic carbon chains seen. This result implies that the Warm Carbon Chain Chemistry (WCCC, e.g. N. Sakai & S. Yamamoto 2013) might trace outflows rather than infall. The formation of aliphatic chains in the disk wind could promote the abundant aliphatic organics found in meteorites and asteroids.

AI.tldr: JWST spectral analysis of the Class I protostar HOPS-68 reveals a hot inner-disk "refractory carbon destruction zone" releasing carbon that a disk wind redistributes outward, potentially explaining Earth's carbon depletion and the origin of aliphatic organics.
AI.motivation: Earth's surface and deep mantle are strongly carbon-depleted relative to solar abundances. One proposed mechanism is thermal sublimation of solid carbonaceous material in the inner midplanes of young disks. The authors use HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with a rich hydrocarbon spectrum, as a testbed to study this thermal processing.
AI.method: Analysis of the JWST spectrum of HOPS-68 using local thermal equilibrium (LTE) slab models to characterize carbon-bearing species, complemented by ALMA observations of C2H. A companion study established that the source recondenses refractory dust from a hot inner-disk region and that oxygen species trace a 300-500 K molecular layer entrained in a disk wind.
AI.result: Warm (~400 K) HCN and C2H2 are detected at the base of a disk wind, while colder (~40 K) C4H2, CH3, and CS are found in the outer disk or outflow cavity wall. 13CCH2, CH4, and C6H2 are also detected, and ALMA shows C2H tracing outflow cavity walls.

The disk wind redistributes carbon (via HCN and C2H2) to the colder outer disk, where UV-induced gas-phase reactions with C2H in outflow cavity walls form aliphatic carbon chains. This implies Warm Carbon Chain Chemistry (WCCC) may trace outflows rather than infall, and that aliphatic chain formation in disk winds could promote the abundant aliphatic organics found in meteorites and asteroids.

title: X-rays from Low-mass Active Galaxies in the Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present new Chandra observations of seven broad-line AGNs in low-mass galaxies ($M_\star < 5 \times 10^9\,M_\odot$) selected from the GAMA sample of Salehirad et al. (2022). X-ray emission is detected in six galaxies, with luminosities spanning $\log(L_{\rm 0.5-8\,keV}/{\rm erg\,s^{-1}})\approx40.5$--43.8. Their X-ray luminosities generally exceed predictions for X-ray binary populations, and their proximity to the optical galaxy nuclei favors accreting massive black holes as the dominant emission source. Spectral fits for four sources yield photon indices $Γ\approx1.7$--2.2, with little evidence for intrinsic absorption in most cases. Virial black hole masses and hard X-ray bolometric corrections imply nominal Eddington ratios $λ_{\rm Edd}\approx0.004$--1.1, although uncertainties are substantial. Optical tracers generally imply higher bolometric luminosities and Eddington ratios, particularly for the X-ray-undetected galaxy. The X-ray-bright sources are broadly consistent with optical AGN scaling relations involving H$α$ and [O III], whereas most lie below the established X-ray--mid-infrared relation, potentially reflecting host-galaxy contamination. Four sources are consistent with the expected UV-to-X-ray spectral slope relation, while three show evidence for relative X-ray weakness. These results reveal diverse X-ray properties among broad-line AGNs in low-mass galaxies and highlight the importance of multiwavelength diagnostics for understanding black hole accretion and interpreting broad-line AGN candidates at high redshift.

AI.tldr: Chandra observations of seven broad-line AGNs in low-mass GAMA galaxies detect X-rays in six, revealing diverse accretion properties and highlighting multiwavelength diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Broad-line AGN candidates in low-mass galaxies serve as local analogs for early black hole growth and high-redshift AGN selection, yet their X-ray properties are poorly characterized.
AI.method: New Chandra X-ray observations plus spectral fitting, virial BH mass estimates, hard X-ray bolometric corrections, Eddington ratios, and comparison with optical (H-alpha, [O III]), mid-IR, and UV-to-X-ray slope relations.
AI.result: Six of seven galaxies detected, log L(0.5-8 keV) ~ 40.5-43.8 erg/s; four sources with photon indices Gamma ~ 1.7-2.2 and little absorption; Eddington ratios ~0.004-1.1 with large uncertainties; optical tracers imply higher bolometric luminosities; most sources lie below the X-ray-mid-IR relation; four consistent with UV-to-X-ray slope relation, three show relative X-ray weakness.

title: A Detailed Polarimetric Imaging Study of Type II Solar Radio Burst with the MWA: Detection of Linear Polarization
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal Letters, under review
summary: Type II radio bursts, produced by magnetohydrodynamic shocks propagating through the solar corona and interplanetary medium, serve as powerful diagnostics of shock properties and ambient coronal magnetic fields. While circular polarization in type II bursts has been extensively studied, most investigations rely on dynamic spectra (DS), providing only spatially integrated measurements. DS obscures spatial variations of the polarization sign and magnitude, potentially causing cancellation effects and misrepresenting true polarization levels. We present a full-polarimetric imaging study of a metric type II burst observed with the Murchison Widefield Array at 78--133 MHz. Remarkably, we report the first detection of linear polarization in a metric type II burst, reaching a polarization fraction of $\sim12\%$ with significant spectro-temporal variability across observing bands. The spectro-temporal, spatial, and morphological properties found in this study establish linear polarization as a new diagnostic of large-scale coronal and interplanetary magnetic field structure through full-Stokes imaging of metric solar radio bursts -- challenging conventional paradigms predicting negligible linear polarization from coherent plasma emission processes.

AI.tldr: First full-polarimetric imaging of a metric type II radio burst with the MWA reveals linear polarization (~12%) that challenges the assumption of negligible linear polarization from coherent plasma emission.
AI.motivation: Type II bursts diagnose shock properties and coronal magnetic fields, but prior polarization studies relied on dynamic spectra, which integrate spatially and can cancel out opposite polarization signs, misrepresenting true polarization levels. Spatially resolved full-Stokes measurements were lacking.
AI.method: Full-polarimetric imaging of a metric type II burst observed with the Murchison Widefield Array at 78–133 MHz, examining spectro-temporal, spatial, and morphological polarization properties.
AI.result: First detection of linear polarization in a metric type II burst, with a polarization fraction of ~12% and significant spectro-temporal variability across observing bands.
AI.conclusion: Linear polarization is established as a new diagnostic of large-scale coronal and interplanetary magnetic field structure via full-Stokes imaging of metric solar radio bursts, challenging the paradigm predicting negligible linear polarization from coherent plasma emission.

title: He I $λ$10830 Resonant Scattering in M17: Toward a Diagnostic of Optical Depth and Gas Kinematics
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ApJL
summary: The lower level of the He I $λ$10830 transition is metastable and therefore well populated. In H II regions, the line can become optically thick, and its photons then undergo resonant scattering. Draine (2026) predicted that scattering splits the profile into several peaks. We present Magellan/WINERED spectra ($R \approx 70{,}000$) at six pointings along a line from the ionizing source CEN 1 across the southwestern bar of M17, with He I $λ$10830 and Pa$γ$ in the same exposures. Every He I $λ$10830 profile is multi-peaked, while the Pa$γ$ profiles are single-peaked. Because Pa$γ$ does not undergo resonant scattering, it traces gas kinematics; its single peak argues against a purely kinematic origin of the He I peaks, and the shared exposures exclude an instrumental origin. We therefore attribute the He I peaks to resonant scattering, as predicted. We compare the profiles quantitatively with the static, spherically symmetric models of Draine (2026), using width and asymmetry measures independent of the systemic velocity. At two pointings far from CEN 1, no static model of any optical depth reproduces width and asymmetry together: both profiles are more red-weighted than static models of comparable width. Such profiles cannot arise from uniform motion but are expected from scattering in expanding gas. We argue that the profile is shaped by both the kinematics and the optical depth of the He$^{+}$ zone, and resolved He I $λ$10830 profiles could therefore provide a new diagnostic of these properties in H II regions.

AI.tldr: Multi-peaked He I λ10830 profiles in M17 H II regions are attributed to resonant scattering (not kinematics or instrumental effects), and two distant pointings require expanding gas rather than static models.
AI.motivation: The metastable lower level of He I λ10830 makes the line optically thick in H II regions, so its photons resonantly scatter; Draine (2026) predicted such scattering splits the profile into multiple peaks, but this had not been tested observationally.
AI.method: High-resolution Magellan/WINERED spectra (R ≈ 70,000) at six pointings from the ionizing source CEN 1 across the southwestern bar of M17, with He I λ10830 and Paγ in the same exposures. Profiles are compared quantitatively with static, spherically symmetric Draine (2026) models using width and asymmetry measures independent of systemic velocity.
AI.result: All He I λ10830 profiles are multi-peaked while Paγ profiles are single-peaked; since Paγ is non-resonantly scattered and traces kinematics, and shared exposures exclude instrumental effects, the He I peaks are attributed to resonant scattering. At two pointings far from CEN 1, no static model of any optical depth reproduces width and asymmetry together; both profiles are more red-weighted than comparable-width static models.
AI.conclusion: The He I λ10830 profile is shaped by both the kinematics and the optical depth of the He+ zone; such red-weighted profiles cannot arise from uniform motion but are expected from scattering in expanding gas. Resolved He I λ10830 profiles may provide a new diagnostic of these properties in H II regions.

title: MAGIC's interferometric diameters of $θ$ Ophiuchi and $β$ CMa and comparison with asteroseismic modelling
summary: $β$ Cephei type stars are massive ($8-25$M$_{\odot}$) and known to have several pulsation modes with periods typically of a few hours. Despite a better understanding of their physics since 1992, the inner structure of these stars involves key stellar physics processes that are still uncertain. Asteroseismology offers insights into these variable stars by analysing pulsation modes, helping to probe their inner layers and understand their structure and mixing processes. We measure the angular diameter of two $β$ Cephei stars, $θ$ Oph and $β$ CMa, using the MAGIC Stellar Intensity Interferometer and compare them, together with the Gaia and Hipparcos parallaxes, to the predictions of the asteroseismic model. The latter are based on Levenberg-Marquardt local minimisation of stellar evolution model parameters to fit observed pulsation modes. In the case of $θ$ Oph, the observed angular diameters are compatible with the asteroseismic model. For $β$ CMa, the radius derived from the angular diameter and the Hipparcos parallax is in tension, at the $2.5σ$ level, with the asteroseismic prediction. We show that this tension mirrors a pre-existing conflict between independent spectroscopic determinations of the surface gravity of the star, that percent-level systematics of the stellar models are quantitatively insufficient to explain it, and that it most likely points to a bias of the Hipparcos parallax. In the frame of this paper, the statistical uncertainty on the interferometric results is similar to the systematic uncertainty on the parallaxes. With the already implemented addition in early 2024 of the first Large-Sized Telescope (CTAO-North LST-1) to the setup, the uncertainty in the angular diameter of these stars is expected to decrease by an order of magnitude, allowing to further constrain stellar evolution models and parallaxes.

AI.tldr: Angular diameters of two β Cephei stars ($\theta$ Oph and β CMa) measured with the MAGIC Stellar Intensity Interferometer are compared with asteroseismic models and parallaxes; a $2.5\sigma$ tension for β CMa points most likely to a Hipparcos parallax bias rather than to stellar-model systematics.
AI.motivation: β Cephei stars are massive pulsators whose internal structure depends on still-uncertain stellar physics (mixing, interior structure). Asteroseismology can probe their interiors, but independent empirical constraints on radius and distance are needed to test the models; interferometric angular diameters combined with parallaxes provide such a test.
AI.method: Angular diameters of $\theta$ Oph and β CMa were measured using the MAGIC Stellar Intensity Interferometer. These were combined with Gaia and Hipparcos parallaxes and compared to asteroseismic models constructed via Levenberg--Marquardt local minimisation of stellar-evolution parameters fitted to observed pulsation modes.
AI.result: For $\theta$ Oph, the observed angular diameter is compatible with the asteroseismic model. For β CMa, the radius derived from the angular diameter and the Hipparcos parallax disagrees with the asteroseismic prediction at the $2.5\sigma$ level. This tension mirrors a pre-existing conflict between independent spectroscopic surface-gravity determinations, and percent-level stellar-model systematics are quantitatively insufficient to explain it, most likely indicating a bias in the Hipparcos parallax. The statistical uncertainty of the interferometric results is comparable to the systematic uncertainty of the parallaxes.
AI.conclusion: The measurements provide an empirical test of asteroseismic models and parallaxes for β Cephei stars, favouring a Hipparcos systematic for β CMa. With the early-2024 addition of the CTAO-North LST-1 to the setup, angular-diameter uncertainties are expected to drop by an order of magnitude, further constraining stellar-evolution models and parallaxes.

title: Estimating LuSEE-Night's Sensitivity to Cα Radio Recombination Lines
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary: Carbon radio recombination lines (CRRLs) arising from the cold neutral medium (CNM) of the interstellar medium are potential foregrounds in the 1-50 MHz band that LuSEE-Night will observe from the lunar far side. CRRLs are sensitive probes of the temperature, density, and radiation field of the CNM, and LuSEE-Night will provide sky-averaged measurements in a poorly explored frequency range. We model CRRLs across this band, accounting for doppler, collisional, and radiation broadening, and we estimate line strengths using two independent methods - fixing either the peak or the frequency-integrated optical depth - applied both uniformly across the sky and with region-dependent values informed by prior low-frequency observations. We simulate LuSEE-Night's expected response to these CRRLs and further convolve the beam-diluted spectra with LuSEE-Night's polyphase-filter-bank spectrometer response, including its zoomed-mode frequency resolution of $\sim$390 Hz, to obtain the expected observed brightness temperature. Using these simulated spectra, we estimate the integration time required to detect individual CRRLs at SNR=5 across the six sky models considered. Required integration times range from as short as 30 hours (in the most optimistic model where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-3}$) to 27.6 years (in the most conservative models where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-4}$). Stacking the 361 simulated C$α$ lines between 10 and 50 MHz reduces the integration time needed for an SNR=5 detection to $\sim$11 minutes and $\sim$151 hours respectively, indicating that LuSEE-Night has realistic chances of making a stacked detection of C$α$ RRLs within a realistic mission lifetime, even under the most conservative optical-depth assumptions.

AI.tldr: This paper models carbon radio recombination lines (CRRLs) in the 1–50 MHz band as foregrounds for LuSEE-Night lunar observations, simulating expected signals to estimate integration times required for detection.
AI.motivation: CRRLs from the cold neutral medium are potential foregrounds in the 1–50 MHz band LuSEE-Night will observe from the lunar far side, and represent sensitive probes of CNM temperature, density, and radiation field in a poorly explored frequency range.
AI.method: The authors model CRRLs across the band accounting for Doppler, collisional, and radiation broadening, estimating line strengths via two independent methods (fixing peak vs. frequency-integrated optical depth), applied uniformly and with region-dependent values from prior low-frequency observations. They simulate LuSEE-Night's response, convolve beam-diluted spectra with the polyphase-filter-bank spectrometer response (zoomed-mode resolution ~390 Hz), and compute expected brightness temperature across six sky models.
AI.result: Required integration times for individual SNR=5 CRRL detection range from 30 hours (optimistic, optical depth ~10⁻³) to 27.6 years (conservative, optical depth ~10⁻⁴). Stacking 361 simulated Cα lines between 10–50 MHz reduces this to ~11 minutes and ~151 hours respectively.
AI.conclusion: LuSEE-Night has realistic prospects for a stacked detection of Cα RRLs within a realistic mission lifetime, even under the most conservative optical-depth assumptions.

title: Solar extreme-ultraviolet waves and other associated solar activities
summary: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) waves are large-scale, tsunami like disturbances on the solar surface associated with eruptive phenomena such as solar flares, filament eruptions, and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Because their strong correlation with major solar eruptions, we present here a comprehensive statistical study of EUV waves and their connections to Moreton waves, CMEs, solar flares, type II radio bursts, and solar energetic particle (SEP) events during Solar Cycle 25 (December 2019-December 2025). This study utilizes EUV data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory and coronagraph data from the Large Angle and Spectrometric Coronagraph onboard Solar and Heliospheric Observatory. Our analysis reveals that 12.3% of the observed EUV waves are associated with Moreton waves, 95% with CMEs, 92.7% associated with flares, 44.3% with metric type II radio bursts, and 11.8% with SEPs. While nearly all EUV waves are linked to CMEs, their association with solar flares varies significantly, ranging from weak B-class events to major X-class flares. Furthermore, the majority of Moreton waves correlate with large- or medium-class flares, with only a small fraction associated with weaker C-class flares. Our findings may contribute to a better understanding of space weather events and, potentially, to their forecasting.

AI.tldr: A statistical survey of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) waves over Solar Cycle 25 (Dec 2019–Dec 2025) finds that nearly all are associated with coronal mass ejections, most with flares, and only small fractions with Moreton waves, type II radio bursts, and solar energetic particles.
AI.motivation: EUV waves are large-scale, tsunami-like disturbances on the solar surface tied to eruptive phenomena (flares, filament eruptions, CMEs). Their strong correlation with major eruptions motivates a comprehensive statistical characterization of their connections to other eruptive and energetic signatures, which could inform space-weather understanding and forecasting.
AI.method: Statistical study using EUV imaging from SDO/AIA and coronagraph data from SOHO/LASCO, cross-matching observed EUV waves during Solar Cycle 25 with Moreton waves, CMEs, solar flares, metric type II radio bursts, and SEP events.
AI.result: Of observed EUV waves, 12.3% are associated with Moreton waves, 95% with CMEs, 92.7% with flares, 44.3% with metric type II radio bursts, and 11.8% with SEPs. Flare associations span weak B-class to major X-class events, while most Moreton waves correlate with large- or medium-class flares and only a small fraction with weaker C-class flares.
AI.conclusion: EUV waves are almost universally linked to CMEs but vary widely in flare association. These association rates may improve understanding and forecasting of space-weather events.

title: Evidence for strong shocks in the ISM of small radio sources
comment: To appear in ApJ Letters. Link to data in Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23326653
summary: Radio jets deposit energy into the interstellar medium of their host galaxies, and while a jet is still confined within the host it is expected to drive shocks through the gas. Broad [OIII] 5007 profiles trace ionized gas that has been disturbed, the [OI]/H-alpha versus [OIII]/H-beta diagram helps distinguish gas photoionized by an AGN from gas excited by shocks, and the high ionization [NeV] 3426 line traces the hard UV continuum of the accretion disk, which shocks only reproduce at very high velocities. We have selected two samples of radio-loud AGN from a cross-match of the VLA Sky Survey with DESI Data Release 1, at 0.15 < z < 0.5 and with [OI] 6300 detected at > 5-sigma: one with projected radio sizes of 10-15 kpc, whose jets are still inside the host, and one with sizes greater than 25 kpc, whose jets have broken out. We fit the [OIII] and [OI] profiles, measure W80, and classify each source on the BPT diagram. The confined sources have broader [OIII] lines, sit systematically closer to the LINER region, and are detected less often in [NeV], and the [NeV] difference is not explained by redshift or dust. The broad components are not systematically blueshifted, so the confined sources are distinguished by line width rather than by outflow velocity. We then discuss how these results indicate that the jets of the confined sources are driving strong shocks through the interstellar medium of their hosts.

AI.tldr: By comparing confined (10–15 kpc) versus broken-out (>25 kpc) radio-loud AGN, the authors find that jets still inside their hosts drive strong shocks through the ISM, evidenced by broader [OIII] lines, LINER-like BPT positions, and rarer [NeV] detection.
AI.motivation: Radio jets deposit energy into their host galaxy's interstellar medium, and while a jet remains confined within the host it is expected to drive shocks. The study tests whether observable signatures of shock-driven gas excitation distinguish jets that are still confined from those that have broken out.
AI.method: Two samples of radio-loud AGN were selected from a cross-match of the VLA Sky Survey with DESI DR1 at 0.15 < z < 0.5 with [OI] 6300 detected at >5σ: a confined sample (projected radio sizes 10–15 kpc) and a broken-out sample (>25 kpc). The authors fit [OIII] and [OI] profiles, measure W80, and classify sources on the BPT diagram; they use broad [OIII] 5007, the [OI]/Hα vs [OIII]/Hβ diagnostic, and the high-ionization [NeV] 3426 line.
AI.result: Confined sources show broader [OIII] lines, lie systematically closer to the LINER region on the BPT diagram, and are detected less often in [NeV]; the [NeV] difference is not explained by redshift or dust. The broad components are not systematically blueshifted, so confined sources are distinguished by line width rather than outflow velocity.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that the jets of confined sources are driving strong shocks through the interstellar medium of their hosts, providing observational evidence for jet-ISM interaction while jets are still inside the galaxy.

title: Eigenfrequency sensitivity in nonadiabatic stellar pulsations
comment: 21 pages, 8 figures
summary: We derive an adjoint formulation of eigenfrequency sensitivity for linear nonadiabatic stellar pulsations, including the frequency dependence of the boundary conditions. Local sensitivity kernels and their cumulative integrals describe the responses of the excitation rate and oscillation frequency to prescribed scaling of the pulsation matrix and its acoustic, thermal and coupling blocks. Applications to selected radial modes of post-AGB envelopes reveal distinct spatial and subsystem sensitivity profiles. In the cool model, the ordinary mode has weak sensitivity near both boundaries for the slow branch outer boundary conditions, whereas the strange mode exhibits pronounced sensitivity in the outer layers. Selected modes of the hotter model also show appreciable outer-layer sensitivity. The block decomposition reveals differing contributions and cancellations in the excitation-rate and oscillation-frequency responses.

AI.tldr: The authors derive an adjoint formulation for eigenfrequency sensitivity of linear nonadiabatic stellar pulsations that accounts for the frequency dependence of boundary conditions, yielding local sensitivity kernels and cumulative integrals for excitation rate and oscillation frequency, validated on radial modes of post-AGB envelope models.
AI.motivation: Understanding how the excitation rate and oscillation frequency of nonadiabatic stellar pulsations respond to perturbations across spatial regions and physical subsystems requires a principled sensitivity framework, but existing treatments neglect the frequency dependence of the boundary conditions.
AI.method: An adjoint formulation of eigenfrequency sensitivity is developed for linear nonadiabatic stellar pulsations, explicitly incorporating boundary conditions' frequency dependence. Local sensitivity kernels and their cumulative integrals quantify responses of excitation rate and oscillation frequency to prescribed scaling of the pulsation matrix, decomposed into acoustic, thermal, and coupling blocks.
AI.result: Applications to selected radial modes of post-AGB envelopes show distinct spatial and subsystem sensitivity profiles. In the cool model, the ordinary mode is weakly sensitive near both boundaries under slow-branch outer boundary conditions, while the strange mode is strongly sensitive in the outer layers. Selected modes of the hotter model also show appreciable outer-layer sensitivity. Block decomposition reveals differing contributions and cancellations between excitation-rate and frequency responses.
AI.conclusion: The adjoint sensitivity framework, with its block decomposition, provides a systematic tool for diagnosing where and through which physical subsystems stellar pulsation frequencies and excitation rates are controlled, highlighting contrasting behavior between ordinary and strange modes and the role of boundary-condition frequency dependence.

title: Interstellar and intergalactic medium in the ultraviolet band
comment: accepted to Astronomy Reports, vol 11, 2026
